5 A MESSAGE FROM AMY SAMPLE PBS Business Intelligence is pleased to present you with the ninth annual Audience Insight report. This year’s edition features more content speciﬁ cally requested by readers, including data around diversity (pg. 25), in-depth media trends (pgs. 9-15), and an expanded look at Average Minute Delivery with increased analysis. The COVID-19 pandemic is ﬁ rst and foremost in our thoughts, though it was not the only event that helped shape this past season, one unlike any other in recent memory. It did, however, act as an accelerant for already existing trends. One example is digital streaming: families found themselves spending more time indoors, which, combined with years of steady OTT adoption and the decreasing price of entry-level streaming devices, led to a sharp increase in digital device usage beginning in March 2020. At the same time, streaming options for consumers continued to grow. New services like Disney+ and Peacock debuted, while old favorites Netﬂ ix, YouTube, Amazon Prime, and Hulu continued to generate the bulk of streaming activity. Despite a brief resurgence in live linear TV during initial COVID stay-at-home orders, the boost proved temporary as primetime HUTs fell their typical -5% season-over-season. As a result, most networks – including PBS – continued to experience linear audience ebbs, with only cable news networks consistently bucking the trend. By the time this book reaches you, Passport will have celebrated its ﬁ fth birthday. Since launching in December 2015, this powerful member beneﬁ t has been enjoyed to the tune of more than 106 million streams and more than 2.9 million activations. Passport saw a large upswing in usage during the early days of the pandemic, reaching an all-time high for streams in April 2020. We hope that you will use this book as one part of your decision-making toolkit while also helping you understand the behaviors of the PBS audience. As always, we welcome your feedback and look forward to working with you in the coming year. Amy Sample Vice President, Business Intelligence

Part 02 AUDIENCE OVERVIEW 9 01 THE MEDIA LANDSCAPE Part 01 THE MEDIA LANDSCAPE The season began in Fall 2019 much as recent seasons had, with familiar trends in video content consumption stretching into yet another year. But January 2020 ushered in a year that proved, in more ways than could have been imagined, to be like no other in history (pgs. 6-7). The global Coronavirus pandemic upended the lives of everyone. Almost in an instant, schools and businesses that were able swapped the real for the virtual. Suddenly individuals and families were frozen in place, and Internet bandwidth became nearly as precious as heat or electricity. March saw a surge in content viewing to all outlets, PBS included, as lockdowns spread across the country (pg. 10). And increases on streaming platforms held up through the Spring and Summer. New platforms and technologies that were already proliferating at breakneck pace advanced further during the season, offering homebound audiences more ways to view on their own schedules (pg. 11). The multitude of non-linear options led to more cords being cut, as broadband-only homes grew to 17 million, more than one in ten TV households for the ﬁ rst time, and up from 12 million just a year prior (pg. 11). Daily time spent with media increased such that now half of every adult’s 24-hour day was spent engaged with some sort of media device, driven by signiﬁ cant upticks in viewing and listening on ever-present smartphones and tablets. The competition for eyeballs has expanded well beyond the other major broadcast networks and cable channels. There are well over 200 million subscribers to one or more video services, with Netﬂ ix alone accounting for more than a third of the hours that people spend streaming. Free, ad-supported video options have also multiplied, led by the Roku Channel with more than 43 million users, FOX-owned Tubi with 33 million, and Viacom’s PlutoTV with nearly 27 million users (pg. 12). So, even as PBS holds on to its seventh-place rank among the top 30 TV networks on the basis of primetime household ratings (pg. 13), its cumulative audience on linear platforms will continue to contract as streaming moves closer to becoming the preferred way to deliver content to a television set during primetime. For the past several years, PBS Business Intelligence has predicted the time when digital viewing will surpass linear viewing during primetime (pg. 15). Our original projection of mid-2022 for the general public has been strikingly durable. The PBS audience has been somewhat slower than the general population to engage on digital platforms, but they’re catching up: Among PBS viewers, we expect the digital contribution to primetime viewing to surpass the linear contribution sometime in 2025.

Part 02 AUDIENCE OVERVIEW 17 PBS ﬁ nished the 2019-20 season with an average primetime household rating of 1.15, down 7% from the previous season. While nightly ratings were stable on Thursdays and Saturdays, and up slightly on Fridays, declines on other nights of the week were in the vicinity of 10%. The year-over-year changes would surely have been more signiﬁ cant without the stay-at-home orders that began in earnest during March, when monthly ratings averages began tracking nearly even with the previous season, thus mitigating the downturn (pg. 19). Also in March, streaming got a major boost, particularly among ﬂ agship news and public affairs programs, PBS NewsHour and FRONTLINE (pg. 21). Interest in COVID-19 triggered the trend, and the police killing of unarmed Black man George Floyd in May and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests kept it going. During the summer, as Election Season kicked into high gear and false narratives fueled political ﬁ res, a news-thirsty public increasingly sought out timely, truthful information and insightful analysis—which they seem to have found on PBS. Overall, PBS’s top-rated ongoing primetime series was the durable Call the Midwife, offering a great example of cross- platform viewing, with substantial portions of its average minute delivery (AMD) coming from linear TV, DVR and digital streaming (pg. 20). Antiques Roadshow continued to generate the highest ratings among PBS series on linear TV, even if its digital footprint continues to be relatively small (pg. 22). An average of 55.6 million viewers a month were reached by PBS linear channels during the season. But it is striking to see that the general audience platform with the next largest reach was PBS Digital Studios on its YouTube channels, viewed by nearly 23 million persons a month. Popular video shorts on a broad range of topics in nature, science, health, history, and popular culture generated nearly 56 million streams during the 2019-2020 season. The episode “Why Megalodon (Deﬁ nitely) Went Extinct,” for example, has been viewed nearly 15 million times since ﬁ rst being released two years ago (pgs. 21, 30). The composition of PBS audiences on digital and linear platforms continues to differ markedly, especially in terms of age. While nearly two thirds of PBS TV viewers are over the age of 65, approximately one in ﬁ ve digital users are. Conversely, while nearly half of the PBS digital audience is between the ages of 18 and 49, only 13% of the PBS TV audience is under 50 (pg. 24). Similarly, while only one in four of self-identiﬁ ed contributors to local PBS stations are under the age of 50, nearly 40% of active PBS Passport users are in the same age cohort. It’s clear that distribution of PBS content on the full range of digital platforms is a key not only to maintaining reach but also ensuring ﬁ nancial sustainability into the future. The 2019-2020 season saw increased attention to diversity, equity, and inclusion in all sectors of society, media included. While PBS has continued to match or exceed its overall standing in over-the-air, low-income, and rural households speciﬁ cally, its usage in Asian, Hispanic, and Black households is not at the same level. That said, broadly popular titles like Ken Burns’ Country Music did as well in racially diverse households as they did overall, as did the Skip Gates series Finding Your Roots, which was the top-rated PBS series in Black households, and second from the top in Hispanic ones (pg. 25). 02 GENERAL AUDIENCE OVERVIEW

18 AUDIENCE INSIGHT 2020 HOW TO READ GLOSSARY OF TERMS Rating or AA (Average Audience) - Percent of all TV households (or persons) watching during an average minute of a program or time period. • For the 2019-20 season, each 1.0 household rating point translates into 1,206,000 households watching in an average minute. • The primetime rating includes tuning to all PBS stations, including multi-casts, during an average minute from Monday - Sunday, 8PM- 11PM, plus all DVR playback within seven days. Cume or Cumulative Audience - The unduplicated viewers (typically P2+) to a program, series, or genre. % of Primetime Viewers That Watch - Of everyone aged 2+ that PBS reached in primetime, this represents the percentage of that audience that tuned in at least once to the designated program/ genre. Percent Viewers That Watch is a measure of program/genre exposure amongst our viewing base, rather than a contribution to the overall PBS primetime cume. Stream – Any time a video starts playing. If the video includes a pre-roll, a stream is counted only after the pre-roll ﬁ nishes. Episode Streams – Episode streams are for original broadcasts only and include views for a four-week period after the broadcast TV air date. Live+7 – Includes all playback on a DVR within 7 days of the program feed or original time period. Cross-Platform Average Minute Delivery (AMD) – A proprietary PBS metric that aggregates the number of viewers watching a particular program - across both linear and digital platforms - during any given minute. For those familiar with AA delivery as a standard Nielsen measure, AMD is simply an extension of this concept that includes all available sources of viewing. Part 02 AUDIENCE OVERVIEW 21 Business Intelligence’s goal is to capture PBS viewing activity across as many platforms as possible and use that information to better understand the role each platform plays in maintaining public television’s collective reach and engagement. The cross-platform Average Minute Delivery (see left- hand chart) metric provides an equivalent perspective of PBS general audience viewing across linear television and streaming platforms. Each section of the stacked bar chart represents viewers per minute of programming, analogous to traditional Nielsen AA delivery. We’re increasingly learning that high proportions of DVR and/or streaming (“consumer-driven viewing”) are indicative of promotional success and viewer loyalty, and have the potential to shift series rankings. Reviewing the AMD ranker for the past two seasons, we can see that while live linear viewing still accounts for the bulk of PBS viewing, many series experienced live linear losses that were in step with larger marketplace trends. At the same time, most PBS series saw an uptick in DVR and/or streaming. In a few cases (e.g.,Call the Midwife and Firing Line), year- over-year growth in consumer-driven viewing was enough to successfully offset live linear declines. However, the fact that consumer-driven offsets are not yet a common phenomenon for PBS - coupled with the knowledge that most streamers gravitate towards large services (see pg. 12) - reinforces the importance of ongoing digital distribution efforts. As a case in point, several news and public affairs series were able to substantially augment their audiences last season via YouTube and Facebook. Note: Audience/viewing data for the PBS Amazon Channels are not available at this time. Part 02 AUDIENCE OVERVIEW 25 Collectively, PBS stations (primary stations + subchannels) reach an expansive audience representative of the U.S. population. However, the levers behind this reach vary, and opportunities exist to improve PBS consideration among several target groups. Promisingly, recent incremental shifts in audience size/composition at the individual series level suggest that ongoing diversity efforts are bearing fruit. PBS subchannels currently serve as a signiﬁ cant source of diverse viewers, although that balance may shift as the KIDS 24/7 service matures and children increasingly choose streaming over linear TV viewing. On the general audience side, broadly-appealing PBS non-ﬁ ction series and events tend to draw the largest number of diverse viewers, while targeted programming often attracts a comparatively high proportion of diverse viewers. Ultimately, both approaches may be key to developing and maintaining an inclusive fanbase. Part 02 AUDIENCE OVERVIEW 69 2020 continued a trend that was already underway: children are migrating from linear to non-linear TV viewing experiences and from TVs to digital devices. With the onset of the coronavirus pandemic in the spring, time at home increased along with screen time. Following the initial spring surge, linear TV viewing behavior quickly returned to normal patterns, yet digital consumption continued at an elevated level both overall and for PBS speciﬁ cally. Historically, PBS had been sheltered from the TV viewing declines due to a loyal audience in homes receiving their TV signal via antenna, also known as over-the-air homes. PBS reached more 2-8 year olds in low-income homes, and more Black and Hispanic children, than any of the linear kids’ cable TV networks this season, although viewers are increasingly tuning to non-linear content. Today, 96% of children in TV homes have streaming capabilities, including those in over-the-air homes, so they have many more viewing options available to them than watching via an antenna alone. As a result, across the 2019-20 TV season, PBS ratings declined by 22% and average monthly reach declined by 16% among children ages 2-8. This follows a similar trend across the industry: linear TV viewing declined by 15% overall among children 2-8. Looking ahead, children will likely spend more time streaming content to their TV screens than viewing linear TV by mid-2021. As the children’s media landscape continues its shift towards digital content, the PBS KIDS digital audience and overall streaming have both increased year-over-year. Average monthly digital users grew by 19%, and monthly streams grew by 25%, driven in large part by increased consumption during the pandemic which may stabilize as health-related restrictions are lifted. During this season, PBS KIDS successfully launched Xavier Riddle and the Secret Museum, Hero Elementary, Elinor Wonders Why, a reboot of Clifford the Big Red Dog, and Esme & Roy.
